title: ATP Singles Ranking
text:
The ATP singles ranking is a point-based system that ranks men’s professional tennis players based on their performance in official singles tournaments over the preceding 52 weeks. A player’s best 19 tournament results determines their ranking, with points awarded based on the level of the tournament (e.g., Grand Slam, ATP Masters 1000, ATP 500, ATP 250, etc.) and how far a player advances. Points from tournaments are dropped after 52 weeks and replaced with current performances, meaning rankings can change weekly. Rankings are important for tournament eligibility and their seeding within the draw. The player with the highest number of points at the end of the year is crowned the year-end No. 1 player.

The “Big 3”—Novak Djokovic, Rafael Nadal, and Roger Federer—have been dominating the ATP Tour for the past two decades, a testament to their consistent presence at the top of the singles rankings.

The visualization below illustrates the career trajectory for these players’ singles rankings, with circles denoting their Grand Slam victories at each point in time. Federer dominated the early years, particularly from 2005-2010, as shown by a cluster of green circles coinciding with his peak ranking. On the other hand, Nadal’s Grand Slam wins appear to be more evenly distributed across his career, without any distinct ‘domination’ period. Djokovic, meanwhile, seems to find his prime later than both Federer and Nadal, reflecting his later rise to the top and younger age compared to the other two.










The “New 2”—Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner—have risen to the top of the game in the last few years, bringing new faces to the men’s tennis landscape. Both have established themselves as standouts of the younger generation, challenging the dominance of older players.

The visualization below shows the ATP singles ranking trajectory for Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner, with circles representing their Grand Slam wins. Alcaraz emerged as a frontrunner, rising to the top of the game slightly before Sinner, accumulating a few more Grand Slam titles during this time period. However, Sinner has recently surged ahead in the rankings, signaling the beginning of a fierce rivalry for the world No. 1 spot between these two rising stars.










Beyond visualizing the movement of these five players’ singles rankings over time, we can also examine the percentage of weeks each player has spent at the No. 1 spot throughout their career. The bar chart below highlights this data, showcasing how Djokovic has spent approximately 37.1% of his career as the world No. 1. This is evidence of his sustained dominance at the top of the game and consistency year after year, as rankings are a great data-driven measure of performance based on a player’s results against a variety of different opponents.

It is also interesting to note how Djokovic, Federer, and Nadal make up around 80% of the total weeks spent at No. 1 in their careers. This remarkable statistic not only underscores their individual dominance, but their role in defining modern men’s tennis.

title: Leading Country
text:
The visualization below explores the historical match-win totals for five leading tennis nations, the United States, Spain, France, Italy, and Germany, spanning from 1968 to 2025. This broader international perspective highlights how different eras of tennis greatness have been shaped by the strength of national player cohorts. The United States stands out most prominently in the earlier decades, showing a dramatic peak in match wins throughout the 1970s and 1980s. This reflects a golden generation of American tennis led by icons such as Jimmy Connors, John McEnroe, and later Pete Sampras and Andre Agassi.

As we move toward the 2000s, a noticeable shift occurs in the competitive landscape. Match-win totals across countries become more balanced, signaling globalization of the sport and the rise of strong tennis cultures beyond the United States. Spain emerges as a new powerhouse, driven by clay-court depth and the sustained success of Rafael Nadal and other top Spanish players. France, Italy, and Germany all remain steady contenders, collectively contributing to an increasingly competitive field where success is distributed more evenly across nations.

This graph not only demonstrates the changing dominance in men’s tennis over time but also reflects how the rise of new generations and training infrastructures around the world continues to reshape the sport’s competitive dynamics.











As the era of the “Big 3” comes to a close, the rise of young stars like Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner signals a new chapter in men’s tennis. With their rapid climb to the top of the rankings and early Grand Slam success, they appear poised to reshape the competitive landscape, continuing the trend of a more globally distributed field. Instead of a single dominant nation or trio of players, the future of tennis may be defined by tighter rivalries, more frequent shifts at the top, and increased representation from emerging tennis countries. This transition suggests a sport entering a more unpredictable and thrilling era, one where the next generation has the opportunity to redefine what sustained excellence looks like on the global stage.

title: Home Court Advantage
text:
In tennis, home-court advantage refers to the competitive boost a player may experience when competing in their home country or in familiar playing conditions. This can include things like local crowds supporting their favorite players, reduced travel fatigue, and better acclimation to court speed, climate, and time zone. At major tournaments like the Grand Slams, these factors can subtly but meaningfully influence performance, helping players sustain energy through long matches, feel more confident under pressure, and even benefit from crowd-driven momentum during key points.

The visualization below compares American players’ win percentages at the US Open and the Australian Open from 2000 to 2025, offering insight into potential home-court advantage over time. In the early 2000s, the US Open consistently favored American talent, with win rates hovering above 60% and peaking near 70%. However, that advantage noticeably eroded throughout the 2010s, with performance at both tournaments converging around the 40–50% mark as global competition intensified.
Interestingly, the past few years show a resurgence, particularly at the Australian Open, where American win percentages have climbed sharply again. This shift may reflect the emergence of a new generation of U.S. players who can succeed on multiple surfaces, reducing the historical reliance on hard-court familiarity and New York crowd support. Together, these trends suggest that while home-court advantage remains a factor in Grand Slam performance, American competitiveness is increasingly defined by adaptability and rising young talent capable of winning anywhere in the world.

title: Team Tennis
text:
Since 1963, tennis has given us legends, rivalries, and unforgettable matches. This site brings those stories to life through data visualized in ways that highlight patterns, rivalries, and the evolution of the sport.
At the center of modern tennis history stand Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal, and Novak Djokovic—the Big Three. Their rivalry has defined an era, producing countless classics and pushing each player to new heights. Together, they’ve amassed dozens of Grand Slam titles, spent record-breaking weeks at World No. 1, and redefined what dominance looks like in tennis.
Alongside them, a new generation has begun to take the stage. Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner are not just rising stars, they’re the future of the sport. With data-driven insights, we’ll explore how their early careers compare to the Big Three, and what their budding rivalry might mean for tennis in the years ahead.
Our data stretches back over six decades and includes every player since 1963,their names, heights, countries of origin, and more. By combining rich historical records with modern performance metrics, this project offers both context and clarity to tennis’s biggest debates.

title: Team Tennis
text:
Get to know the players:

Roger Federer Roger Federer is a Swiss tennis player, born in 1981 in Basel, who became one of the sport’s greatest champions with 20 Grand Slam titles,highlighted by a record 8 at Wimbledon. He held the world No. 1 ranking for 310 weeks, earned Olympic medals, and retired in 2022 after more than two decades at the top of the game.


Rafael Nadal Rafael Nadal is a Spanish tennis legend, born in 1986 in Manacor, Mallorca. He turned pro in 2001 and over his career amassed 22 Grand Slam singles titles, including a record 14 at the French Open. He has 92 ATP singles titles total, spent 209 weeks as world No. 1, and dominated especially on clay courts before retiring in 2024.


Novak Djokovic Novak Djokovic is a Serbian tennis player, born in 1987 in Belgrade, who has won a record 24 Grand Slam titles, including 10 Australian Opens. He held the world No. 1 ranking for a record 428 weeks, and established himself as one of the most accomplished and dominant players in tennis history.


Carlos Alcarz Carlos Alcaraz is a Spanish tennis player, born in 2003 in El Palmar, Murcia, who turned professional in 2018 and by age 22 has already won six Grand Slam singles titles — French Open (2024, 2025), Wimbledon (2023, 2024), and US Open (2022, 2025) — and has risen to the world No. 1 ranking (first achieved in 2022 and again in 2025).


Jannik Sinner Jannik Sinner is an Italian tennis player, born in 2001 in San Candido, who turned pro in 2018 and by age 24 has already won 4 Grand Slam singles titles (Australian Open 2024 & 2025, US Open 2024, Wimbledon 2025), reached world No. 1 ranking in 2024, and claimed 24 ATP Tour-level singles titles overall, marking him as one of the rising stars and most accomplished young players in men’s tennis.

title: ATP Doubles
text:
In tennis, doubles involves two teams of two players competing on one court. Unlike singles, where players compete alone, doubles requires teamwork, communication, and a slightly different set of skills. The court is wider in doubles, with both alleys in play, allowing for different angles and more space to attack and defend. Doubles players often have great volleys, quick reflexes, and a wider range of different shots in their repertoire. Being able to react quickly during fast exchanges is a big part of what makes doubles so exciting to watch. Playing doubles often enhances a player’s net game in singles, which is why so many of the top singles players continue to compete in doubles tournaments.

The visualization below shows the number of doubles titles each of our featured players has won over the course of their career. In comparison to their impressive singles achievements, the number of doubles titles they’ve earned are minimal. Rafael Nadal has the most doubles titles to his name, with 11 over the course of his career. Roger Federer is not far behind with 8 doubles titles, and Novak Djokovic only has 1. Although both Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner are at the early stages in their career, they both have zero doubles titles. The average number of doubles titles among these five players are 4.











The graph below shows that these players have not dominated the doubles tour as much as they have in the singles tour. As the caption mentions, the solid colors represent the percentage of doubles matches won, while the faded colors represent matches lost. Federer and Nadal barely have a wining record, whereas Djokovic and Sinner have a losing record. Alcaraz has not played any doubles matches at this point in his career. The ATP tour has doubles specialists—players that only focus on training and playing doubles. Our featured players focus on playing singles, which is why their winning record in doubles is not as impressive.











Although these players have played a few doubles tournaments in their career, it is important to take a look at the timing of these matches. The visualization below shows the total number of doubles matches the Big 3 have played per year. Sinner and Alcaraz have not played enough doubles matches to be included in this visualization. Federer played the most out of everyone at the start of his career, with around 40 total doubles matches in the year 2000. This number just gradually decreased as his career progressed. The dotted lines represent the year each player won their first singles grand slam. It is interesting to note how the number of doubles matches they each played began to decrease after their singles career took off. The Big 3’s shift away from doubles reflects a common pattern among top singles players—as their career goals become focused on overall singles dominance.











Finally, the visualization below puts into perspective the number of matches each player has played in singles (solid colors) vs doubles (faded colors). It is clear that the majority of their career has been spent playing singles tournaments. While doubles tennis has its own set of champions, the spotlight in the sport is overwhelmingly focused on the singles players, especially these five.

title: Tennis
text:
Homework #6: Lindsay Eisenman

Limitations associated with the below visualization:  - Only includes data from the years 2022-2025 and top 10 rankings  - Infrequent changes in the data result in flat sections in the graph  - Difficult to draw meaningful conclusions about performance from rankings 

Here is the code created to clean the Alcaraz and Sinner data:
cleaneddata_alcaraz <- cleaned_rankings_data %>%  mutate(dob = as.Date(as.character(dob), format = “%Y%m%d”)) %>%  mutate(ranking_date = as.Date(as.character(ranking_date), format = “%Y%m%d”)) %>%  mutate(height = as.numeric(height)) %>%  filter(name_last == “Alcaraz”) %>%  filter(name_first == “Carlos”) %>%  mutate(age = as.numeric((ranking_date - dob) / 365.25))  cleaneddata_alcaraz 
cleaneddata_sinner <- cleaned_rankings_data %>%  mutate(dob = as.Date(as.character(dob), format = “%Y%m%d”)) %>%  mutate(ranking_date = as.Date(as.character(ranking_date), format = “%Y%m%d”)) %>%  mutate(height = as.numeric(height)) %>%  filter(name_last == “Sinner”) %>%  filter(name_first == “Jannik”) %>%  mutate(age = as.numeric((ranking_date - dob) / 365.25))  cleaneddata_sinner 

Here is the code to create the visualization using the aboved cleaned data:
new2_ranking_timeline <- ggplot(mapping = aes(x = ranking_date, y = rank)) +  geom_line(data = cleaneddata_sinner, aes(color = “Sinner”)) +  geom_line(data = cleaneddata_alcaraz, aes(color = “Alcaraz”)) +  labs(x = “Date”, y = “Ranking (1 = Highest)”, color = “Player”,  title = “ATP Singles Ranking: Alcaraz vs Sinner (2022-2025)”) +  scale_color_manual(values = c(“Sinner” = “navy”,  “Alcaraz” = “orange”)) +  scale_x_date(limits = as.Date(c(“2022-01-01”, Sys.Date()))) +  scale_y_reverse(limits = c(10,1),  breaks = 10:1,  labels = scales::number_format(accuracy = 1)) +  annotate(“point”, x = as.Date(“2024-01-28”), y = 4, size = 1) +  annotate(“text”, x = as.Date(“2024-01-28”), y = 4.25,  label = “Australian Open”,  size = 3) + #this adds a point and text to show the sinner’s AO win  annotate(“point”, x = as.Date(“2024-09-6”), y = 1, size = 1) +  annotate(“text”, x = as.Date(“2024-09-6”), y = 1.25, label = “US Open”,  size = 3) +  annotate(“point”, x = as.Date(“2022-09-11”), y = 1, size = 1) +  annotate(“text”, x = as.Date(“2022-09-11”), y = 1.25,  label = “US Open”,  size = 3) +  annotate(“point”, x = as.Date(“2023-09-16”), y = 2, size = 1) +  annotate(“text”, x = as.Date(“2023-09-16”), y = 2.25,  label = “Wimbledon”,  size = 3) +  annotate(“point”, x = as.Date(“2024-06-09”), y = 2, size = 1) +  annotate(“text”, x = as.Date(“2024-06-09”), y = 2.25,  label = “French Open”,  size = 3) +  annotate(“point”, x = as.Date(“2024-07-14”), y = 3, size = 1) +  annotate(“text”, x = as.Date(“2024-07-14”), y = 3.25,  label = “Wimbledon”,  size = 3) +  theme_classic()  new2_ranking_timeline 






Plot 1





I used geom_line for this visualization because this is time-series data and I wanted to visualize the trendline and compare the rankings between both players.

Instead of geom_line, I could have also used geom_smooth what provides the following:   Advantages:  - Automatically fits and displays a trend line that reveal patterns in the data  - Reduces noise by summarizing trends instead of showing every fluctuation  - Good for data sets covering a large time frame  Disadvantages:  - Geom_smooth can oversimplify the data and obscure actual data variability  - Results depend on the chosen smoothing method, which can mislead interpretation 

Decorative elements of this visualization:  - Added bullet points on the trend lines to indicate grand slam wins by each player  - Since there were only 6 bullet points total, the graph did not become overcrowded  - However, if there were more grand slam wins, the graph would not be readable  - Another decorative element I could add would be a color gradient for the player’s age 

This visualization relates to Wilke’s “The principle of proportional ink” which emphasizes that the amount of “ink” should be related to the values the data represents. In this case, the lines are thin and trace the ranking movement per player, which is a good use of ink. However, the bullet points labeling each grand slam both players have won is a possible violation of this principle. Any more additional bullet points may lead to an overcrowded graph.

section: Header Level 2: Tips for linking/displaying figures and images.
text:
Header Level 2: Tips for linking/displaying figures and images.

Header Level 3: Linking to a Plot/Fig

Write you code to create your plot and save it. Save this script in src/figs. The source code does not need to be on the website.
Ensure that your plot is saved to figs/ by referencing the path with {here}.
At the top of the .qmd file for your page, add a code block that source()s the script that will generate the plot you wish displayed on that page.

For example:
source(here::here("figs", "point_mpg_by_wt.R"))`
Make sure to edit the code block so that the code runs only (no output).
NOTE: Code blocks that appear in .qmd files will call .R files only. Do NOT embed code blocks in your .qmd file(s) that will process data or create plots directly. Reserve .qmd files for website text, sourcing script files, and calling .png plot files. Developers and engineers compartmentalize project elements and do not combine all content into a single files. Doing so creates many problems not limited to code breaking and code-repair problems, Git merge problems, etc. You will follow a similar practice of breaking the project into pieces, save those files, and push them to the remote repository weekly for your team members.
This code-source()ing step also ensures that plot(s) are (re)created when Quarto rendering the website build files. You certainly want this feature so that new website elements and files are built during the rendering process. A full website re-build, however, is unnecessary when no element of the website changes other than the images and figures embedded within it. As a result, re-builds are not always necessary and will increase update time.

title: Page example
section: Header Level 2: (Optional) Circumventing a Full Website Build
text:
Header Level 2: (Optional) Circumventing a Full Website Build
Sometimes the main structure of your website is untouched but you have new data and you need to run a rebuild of your plots. Although re-rendering is not problematic, it might just take longer than you desire. If you don’t need to render the website and just want to build files, the following is a solution, though requires some extra work.
To avoid a full site rebuild (re-render) when you simply want to create and git push new plots:

Add your source()ing code to a separate file, for example, call_scripts/call_plot_scripts.qmd.
Add a code block to source individual .R files or all .R files in a directory.

Example:
#| include: false

# source a script file that this page depends on
source(here::here("figs", "point_mpg_by_wt.R"))

This .qmd file will render and create the .png files you need in your specified directory but the page will not be linked on your website. Technically, it will be visible at https://the_url/call_scripts/call_plot_scripts.html but this will be difficult to find. You can always remove the file or directory after rendering the website if you want to remove it completely.


Link the plot .png file in your .qmd file.

The ATP singles ranking is a point-based system that ranks men’s professional tennis players based on their performance in official singles tournaments over the preceding 52 weeks. A player’s best 19 tournament results determines their ranking, with points awarded based on the level of the tournament (e.g., Grand Slam, ATP Masters 1000, ATP 500, ATP 250, etc.) and how far a player advances. Points from tournaments are dropped after 52 weeks and replaced with current performances, meaning rankings can change weekly. Rankings are important for tournament eligibility and their seeding within the draw. The player with the highest number of points at the end of the year is crowned the year-end No. 1 player.

The “Big 3”—Novak Djokovic, Rafael Nadal, and Roger Federer—have been dominating the ATP Tour for the past two decades, a testament to their consistent presence at the top of the singles rankings.

The visualization below illustrates the career trajectory for these players’ singles rankings, with circles denoting their Grand Slam victories at each point in time. Federer dominated the early years, particularly from 2005-2010, as shown by a cluster of green circles coinciding with his peak ranking. On the other hand, Nadal’s Grand Slam wins appear to be more evenly distributed across his career, without any distinct ‘domination’ period. Djokovic, meanwhile, seems to find his prime later than both Federer and Nadal, reflecting his later rise to the top and younger age compared to the other two.










The “New 2”—Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner—have risen to the top of the game in the last few years, bringing new faces to the men’s tennis landscape. Both have established themselves as standouts of the younger generation, challenging the dominance of older players.

The visualization below shows the ATP singles ranking trajectory for Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner, with circles representing their Grand Slam wins. Alcaraz emerged as a frontrunner, rising to the top of the game slightly before Sinner and accumulating a few more Grand Slam titles during this time period. However, Sinner has recently surged ahead in the rankings, signaling the beginning of a fierce rivalry for the world No. 1 spot between these two rising stars.










Beyond visualizing the movement of these five players’ singles rankings over time, we can also examine the percentage of weeks each player has spent at the No. 1 spot throughout their career. The bar chart below highlights this data, showcasing how Djokovic has spent approximately 37.1% of his career as the world No. 1. This is evidence of his sustained dominance at the top of the game and consistency year after year, as rankings are a great data-driven measure of performance based on a player’s results against a variety of different opponents.

It is also interesting to note how Djokovic, Federer, and Nadal make up around 80% of the total weeks spent at No. 1 in their careers. This remarkable statistic not only underscores their individual dominance, but their role in defining modern men’s tennis.
